5.2.1.examLens: How the data are collected decides whether a chart can tell the truth. Know rational subgrouping and the two phases of a control chart's life.

worked.question: Choose the chart for each: (a) one temperature reading per batch, one batch per day; (b) 5 shafts measured every hour; (c) 12 readings from a multi-spindle machine each hour; (d) the number of late shipments out of exactly 200 orders each day; (e) the number of late shipments per day where order volume varies; (f) scratches counted on each 1 square meter panel; (g) defects per invoice, with invoices of different lengths.
worked.solution: (a) I-MR. (b) Xbar-R. (c) Xbar-S (subgroup above about 10). (d) np (constant n, defective units). (e) p (varying n). (f) c (constant area, defect counts). (g) u (varying size, defect counts).

5.2.2.examLens: Use it when readings arrive one at a time. The constants 2.66, 3.267, and 1.128 are worth knowing.

worked.question: Ten daily readings: 10.2, 10.5, 9.8, 10.1, 10.6, 10.0, 9.9, 10.4, 10.3, 10.2. Compute the I-MR limits and estimate σ.
worked.solution:
X̄ = 102.0 ÷ 10 = 10.2.
Moving ranges: 0.3, 0.7, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.1, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1. Sum = 3.2, so MR̄ = 3.2 ÷ 9 = 0.356.
Individuals chart: 10.2 ± 2.66 × 0.356 = 10.2 ± 0.946, so UCL = 11.15, LCL = 9.25.
Moving range chart: UCL = 3.267 × 0.356 = 1.16, LCL = 0.
σ estimate = 0.356 ÷ 1.128 = 0.315. All points are inside the limits.

5.2.3.examLens: The workhorse for continuous data in subgroups. Compute both sets of limits and read the R chart first.

worked.question: A process is sampled in subgroups of n = 4. From 25 subgroups, X̿ = 50.0 and R̄ = 6.0. Find the control limits for both charts and estimate σ.
worked.solution:
From the table, for n = 4: A2 = 0.729, D3 = 0, D4 = 2.282, d2 = 2.059.
Xbar chart: 50.0 ± 0.729 × 6.0 = 50.0 ± 4.37, so UCL = 54.37, LCL = 45.63.
R chart: UCL = 2.282 × 6.0 = 13.69, LCL = 0.
σ estimate = 6.0 ÷ 2.059 = 2.91.

5.2.4.examLens: For counts of defects when the amount inspected varies. Know its twin, the c chart, which is on the sheet.

worked.question: Ten batches of invoices contain 90 errors in total across 300 invoices (average batch size n̄ = 30). (a) Compute the u chart limits. (b) For a c chart with c̄ = 9 defects per unit, compute the limits.

5.2.5.examLens: The standard chart for the proportion of defective units when the sample size changes.

worked.question: Over 10 days, 2,000 units were inspected in total and 120 were defective. Compute the p chart limits using the average sample size.

5.2.6.examLens: The same data as a p chart, plotted as counts, when the sample size is constant.

worked.question: Samples of n = 200 are taken daily, and the long-run defective rate is p̄ = 0.06. Compute the np chart limits.

5.2.7.examLens: For larger subgroups, the standard deviation is a better measure of spread than the range.

worked.question: Subgroups of n = 10 give X̿ = 100.0 and S̄ = 4.0. Find the limits and estimate σ.

5.2.8.examLens: Choose it for small, sustained shifts, and know why a regular Shewhart chart can miss them.

worked.question: The process mean shifts from 50 to 51.5 (σ = 2, a shift of 0.75σ). Individual readings stay well inside the 3σ limits. A CuSum uses k = 0.5σ = 1 and h = 4σ = 8. How many readings until it signals?
worked.solution: Each reading averages 51.5, which is 0.5 above the reference level (50 + 1 = 51). The upper CuSum therefore grows by about 0.5 per reading. It reaches h = 8 after about 16 readings, a signal the individuals chart would likely miss.

5.2.9.examLens: The other small-shift chart. Know the formula and what λ does.

worked.question: Target = 50, λ = 0.2, starting z = 50. Readings: 52, 53, 51. Compute the EWMA values.
worked.solution:
z₁ = 0.2 × 52 + 0.8 × 50 = 50.40.
z₂ = 0.2 × 53 + 0.8 × 50.40 = 10.6 + 40.32 = 50.92.
z₃ = 0.2 × 51 + 0.8 × 50.92 = 10.2 + 40.74 = 50.94.
The statistic drifts upward gradually, which is how EWMA reveals a small sustained shift.

5.2.10.examLens: Older versions of the BOK title this topic "Control Chart Anatomy," so this section covers both: how a chart is built, the rules for reading it, and how to respond.

worked.question: (a) A chart shows nine consecutive points above the center line, all inside the control limits. What is the signal and what do you do? (b) Two of three consecutive points fall beyond 2σ on the same side. Signal? (c) A technician sees one point just outside the limit, finds a known tool breakage, and wants to delete the point and recalculate the limits. Is that right?
worked.solution:
(a) Nelson test 2 (nine in a row on one side): a likely shift in the process mean. Investigate for a special cause even though no point is outside the limits.
(b) A Western Electric / Nelson signal (two of three beyond 2σ). Investigate.
(c) The out-of-limit point has an assignable cause (the broken tool), so it should be investigated and corrected. Recalculate limits only if it is established that the cause has been removed and the process has a stable baseline, and document it. Do not simply delete points to tighten the chart.

5.2.1.a.title: Rational subgrouping
5.2.1.a.html:
Form each subgroup from items made under the same conditions, close together in time, so that variation within a subgroup is only common-cause variation. Then variation between subgroups reveals special causes such as shifts or drift.
Example: take 5 consecutive parts from one machine each hour. Do not mix parts from two machines in one subgroup, because machine differences would hide inside the subgroup.

5.2.1.b.title: Subgroup size and sampling frequency
5.2.1.b.html:
• Subgroup size: commonly 3 to 5 for Xbar-R. Large enough to give a good average, small enough to stay "rational."
  • Frequency: often enough to catch a change before much bad product is made. It depends on how fast the process can change and how costly sampling is.

These choices decide what the chart can detect.

5.2.1.c.title: Variable versus attribute data
5.2.1.c.html: Continuous (variable) data and counted (attribute) data use different charts. The data type is the first step in the selection tree.

5.2.1.d.title: Phase I and Phase II
5.2.1.d.html:
• Phase I: collect data (often about 20 to 25 subgroups, a guideline and not a rule), compute trial limits, find and remove special causes, and settle on the limits.
  • Phase II: use those limits to monitor the process going forward.

5.2.1.e.title: Operational definitions and check sheets
5.2.1.e.html: Define exactly what counts as a defect and how it is measured, so every collector records the same thing. A check sheet is a simple form for recording data consistently as it is collected.

5.2.1.f.title: Pick the chart
5.2.1.f.html: Use the data type and subgroup size and read the chart off the selection tree above.

5.2.1.g.title: The purpose of rational subgrouping
5.2.1.g.html: Maximize the chance that common-cause variation shows up within subgroups, and that special-cause shifts show up between them. A poorly chosen subgroup can hide a problem or invent one.

5.2.2.a.title: What it is
5.2.2.a.html: The individuals and moving range chart. Each plotted point is a single reading (subgroup size 1). The moving range (MR) is the absolute difference between each reading and the one before it.

5.2.2.b.title: The limits
5.2.2.b.html:
• Individuals chart: center = X̄; UCL and LCL = X̄ ± 2.66 × MR̄.
  • Moving range chart: UCL = 3.267 × MR̄; LCL = 0 (D3 is 0 for subgroups below 7).
  • The number 2.66 comes from 3 ÷ 1.128.

5.2.2.d.title: When it is used
5.2.2.d.html: For slow, low-volume, or batch data, where a subgroup is not practical. It is sensitive to non-normality because it works on individual values.

5.2.2.f.title: What is on the sheet
5.2.2.f.html: The I-MR formulas are not on the reference sheet, but the n = 2 row of the constants table gives them: 2.66 = 3 ÷ d2 (d2 = 1.128), and MR chart UCL = D4 × MR̄ = 3.267 × MR̄. Know how to build them from that row.

5.2.3.a.title: What it is
5.2.3.a.html: Two charts together: an Xbar chart (subgroup averages, watching the center) and an R chart (subgroup ranges, watching the spread). Used for subgroups of 2 to 10, commonly 3 to 5.

5.2.3.b.title: The formulas (on the reference sheet)
5.2.3.b.html:
• Grand mean X̿ = ΣX̄ ÷ k, and R̄ = ΣR ÷ k, where k is the number of subgroups.
  • Xbar chart: UCL and LCL = X̿ ± A2 × R̄.
  • R chart: UCL = D4 × R̄, LCL = D3 × R̄.

5.2.3.c.title: The constants (on the sheet)
5.2.3.c.html:
The reference document has a Control Charts Table of Constants for n = 2 to 25. Key rows:

nA2A3d2D3D4B3B4
21.8802.6591.1280.0003.2670.0003.267
31.0231.9541.6930.0002.5750.0002.568
40.7291.6282.0590.0002.2820.0002.266
50.5771.4272.3260.0002.1140.0002.089
100.3080.9753.0780.2231.7770.2841.716

Xbar-R uses A2, D3, D4, and d2. Xbar-S uses A3, B3, and B4. Always use the values in the table you are given, since other published tables round slightly differently.

5.2.3.e.title: Read the R chart first
5.2.3.e.html: Check the R chart (variation) before the Xbar chart (center). If the spread is out of control, the Xbar limits are not reliable.

5.2.3.f.title: Constants
5.2.3.f.html: The sheet gives both the formulas and the constants table. Practice finding the right column (A2 for Xbar-R, A3 for Xbar-S) and the right row (your subgroup size n) quickly.

5.2.4.a.title: What it is
5.2.4.a.html: Plots defects per unit when the sample size or area of opportunity varies. The count follows a Poisson pattern.

5.2.4.b.title: The formulas (reference-sheet form)
5.2.4.b.html:
• ū = Σc ÷ Σn (total defects over total units inspected).
  • n̄ = Σnᵢ ÷ k (average subgroup size).
  • UCL and LCL = ū ± 3 × √(ū ÷ n̄).

Software usually draws limits that vary with each subgroup's own n. For hand calculation, use the sheet's n̄ form unless told otherwise.

5.2.4.c.title: The c chart (on the sheet)
5.2.4.c.html: The c chart counts defects when the area of opportunity is constant. c̄ = total defects ÷ number of subgroups, and limits = c̄ ± 3 × √c̄. The sheet's notation for c̄ is loose, so use the definition above.

5.2.4.d.title: Defects per invoice, different batch sizes

5.2.4.e.title: Negative lower limits
5.2.4.e.html: If the computed LCL is negative, set it to 0, since a count cannot be below zero.

5.2.5.a.title: What it is
5.2.5.a.html: Plots the proportion defective in each sample when the sample size varies. The counts follow a binomial pattern.

5.2.5.b.title: The formulas (reference-sheet form)
5.2.5.b.html:
• p̄ = Σ(np) ÷ Σn (total defectives over total inspected).
  • n̄ = Σnᵢ ÷ k.
  • UCL and LCL = p̄ ± 3 × √[ p̄(1 − p̄) ÷ n̄ ].

Software varies the limits with each subgroup's n.

5.2.5.c.title: Late shipments with varying volume
5.2.5.c.html: The percent of orders shipped late, with changing daily volume, is a p chart.

5.2.5.d.title: Bounds
5.2.5.d.html: If the computed LCL is negative, set it to 0, and the UCL cannot meaningfully exceed 1 (100%).

5.2.6.a.title: What it is
5.2.6.a.html: Plots the number of defective units in each sample when the sample size is constant.

5.2.6.b.title: The formulas
5.2.6.b.html:
• Center = np̄ (average number defective per sample).
  • UCL and LCL = np̄ ± 3 × √[ np̄(1 − p̄) ].

5.2.6.c.title: np or p?
5.2.6.c.html: A constant sample of 200 is an np chart. If the size varies, it is a p chart.

5.2.6.d.title: Bounds
5.2.6.d.html: If the computed LCL is negative, set it to 0. The UCL cannot exceed n.

5.2.7.a.title: What it is
5.2.7.a.html: Like Xbar-R, but the second chart shows the subgroup standard deviation (S). It is used for subgroups above about 10, where the range wastes information.

5.2.7.b.title: The formulas
5.2.7.b.html:
• Xbar chart: UCL and LCL = X̿ ± A3 × S̄.
  • S chart: UCL = B4 × S̄, LCL = B3 × S̄.
  • σ estimate = S̄ ÷ c4. (c4 is not in the sheet's table, so it would have to be supplied.)

5.2.7.c.title: Constants for n = 10
5.2.7.c.html: From the sheet's table at n = 10: A3 = 0.975, B3 = 0.284, B4 = 1.716. (c4 = 0.9727 is not in the table.)

5.2.7.d.title: Subgroup of 15
5.2.7.d.html: Subgroups of 15 readings call for an Xbar-S chart.

5.2.7.e.title: Check the sheet's S chart entry
5.2.7.e.html: The S chart limits are UCL = B4 × S̄ and LCL = B3 × S̄, and the mean chart uses A3 × S̄. (The 2010 copy of the sheet misprinted B4 for both; version 1.4.2 has it right.)

5.2.8.a.title: What it is
5.2.8.a.html: Plots the cumulative sum of deviations from a target. Each new point adds to the running total, so small consistent departures pile up and become visible.

5.2.8.b.title: Strengths
5.2.8.b.html: Detects small, sustained shifts faster than a Shewhart chart (Xbar, individuals). It is slower for large, sudden shifts.

5.2.8.c.title: Parameters
5.2.8.c.html: Typical starting values: a target, a reference value k (about 0.5σ), and a decision interval h (about 4 to 5σ). These are design choices, not fixed thresholds.

5.2.8.d.title: Small persistent drift
5.2.8.d.html: When a question says "detect a small persistent drift," the answer is CuSum or EWMA.

5.2.8.e.title: The CuSum on the reference sheet
5.2.8.e.html:
The sheet gives a standardized version: Sₙ = (1 ÷ σx) × Σ(xᵢ − T), where T is the target and σx the process standard deviation. It is the running total of deviations from target, measured in σ units.
Example: target 50, σ = 2, readings 52, 51, 53. Deviations 2, 1, 3, total 6. S = 6 ÷ 2 = 3.0.

5.2.9.a.title: The formula
5.2.9.a.html: EWMAₜ = λ × Yₜ + (1 − λ) × EWMAₜ₋₁ (this is on the reference sheet), where λ is greater than 0 and at most 1, and EWMA₀ is the target or the historical mean. Each point is a weighted average of the newest reading and all earlier ones, with recent data weighted most.

5.2.9.b.title: The weight λ
5.2.9.b.html: λ is typically 0.05 to 0.25 (a common choice, not fixed). Small λ gives more smoothing and better detection of small shifts. Control limits are about 3σ of the EWMA statistic.

5.2.9.c.title: Strengths
5.2.9.c.html: Detects small shifts, weights recent data more heavily, and is fairly robust to non-normality.

5.2.9.d.title: CuSum, EWMA, or Shewhart?
5.2.9.d.html: For small shifts, favor CuSum or EWMA. For large, sudden shifts, a regular Shewhart chart is fine.

5.2.10.a.title: Western Electric rules
5.2.10.a.html:
A signal is:

  1. One point beyond 3σ.
  2. Two of three points beyond 2σ (same side).
  3. Four of five points beyond 1σ (same side).
  4. Eight in a row on one side of the center line.

5.2.10.b.title: Nelson tests (the Minitab set)
5.2.10.b.html:
1. One point beyond 3σ.
  2. Nine in a row on one side of the center line.
  3. Six in a row steadily increasing or decreasing (a trend).
  4. Fourteen in a row alternating up and down.
  5. Two of three points beyond 2σ (same side).
  6. Four of five points beyond 1σ (same side).
  7. Fifteen in a row within 1σ of the center line (either side), which suggests stratification or limits that are too wide.
  8. Eight in a row beyond 1σ on either side, which suggests a mixture of two populations.

5.2.10.c.title: Common cause versus special cause
5.2.10.c.html:
• Common cause: natural variation. Leave it alone and improve the system if the level is not acceptable.
  • Special cause: an assignable event. Investigate and react.

5.2.10.d.title: Control limits are not spec limits
5.2.10.d.html: Control limits come from the process. Spec limits come from the customer. A 3σ limit gives about a 0.27% false-alarm rate per independent point. Using several sensitizing rules together raises the overall false-alarm rate.

5.2.10.e.title: Chart selection
5.2.10.e.html: By data type and subgroup size (see the selection tree at the top of this file).

5.2.10.f.title: Other control methods
5.2.10.f.html: Charts are one method. Others include standard work, training, documented procedures, audits, and handoff to the process owner.

5.2.10.g.title: Read the chart and choose the action
5.2.10.g.html: Given a chart, name the rule that was violated and decide: investigate (special cause) or leave alone (common cause).

5.2.10.h.title: Anatomy of a control chart
5.2.10.h.html: A chart has the plotted statistic, a center line, and UCL and LCL at ±3σ of the plotted statistic. The space between is divided into zones: Zone A (2 to 3σ), Zone B (1 to 2σ), and Zone C (center to 1σ). The sensitizing rules use these zones. Note that the σ of the data differs from the σ of the statistic: for subgroup means, the plotted statistic has σ ÷ √n.

5.2.10.i.title: Two rule systems
5.2.10.i.html: Western Electric (8 in a row) and Nelson or Minitab (9 in a row) are different rule systems, not contradictory. Use one set per question and do not mix them.

5.2.10.j.title: Time-weighted charts
5.2.10.j.html: Minitab applies only the beyond-the-limits test on time-weighted charts (EWMA and CuSum).

5.2.10.k.title: Do not recompute limits just because a point is out
5.2.10.k.html: Investigate the assignable cause. Recompute limits only after a verified process change and a stable baseline. Deleting points and re-limiting to make a chart look in control hides the problem.

5.2.10.l.title: Inside the limits is not the same as in control
5.2.10.l.html: A point inside the 3σ limits can still violate a run or trend rule. "All points within limits" does not prove control.

5.2.1-1.stem: A team forms each subgroup from 5 parts, taking 2 from machine A and 3 from machine B at the same time. What is the problem?

options.html: Subgroups should always contain one part
Machine differences are hidden inside the subgroup, so a real source of variation will not show between subgroups
Five is too many parts for a subgroup

5.2.1-1.explanation: Within-subgroup variation should be common-cause only. Mixing machines buries a special-cause source inside the subgroup.

5.2.1-2.stem: A team collects about 25 subgroups, calculates trial control limits, finds and removes special causes, and settles the limits. Which phase is this?
5.2.1-2.explanation: Phase I establishes the limits. Phase II uses them to monitor.

5.2.1-3.stem: Twelve readings are taken from a multi-spindle machine each hour. Which chart is best?

5.2.1-4.stem: The number of late shipments is counted out of exactly 200 orders each day. Which chart is best?
5.2.1-4.explanation: Defective units with a constant sample size use an np chart.

5.2.2-1.stem: An individuals chart has X̄ = 20 and a moving range average of 1.5. What are the control limits? (Hint: 3 ÷ d2 = 2.66 for n = 2.)

5.2.3-1.stem: Subgroups of n = 5 give X̿ = 100 and R̄ = 8. What are the Xbar chart limits?

5.2.3-2.stem: Using the same data (n = 5, R̄ = 8), what is the upper control limit of the R chart?
5.2.3-2.explanation: UCL = D4 × R̄ = 2.114 × 8 = 16.91. The lower limit is D3 × R̄ = 0.

5.2.3-3.stem: On an Xbar-R chart, the R chart should be reviewed before the Xbar chart.
5.2.3-3.explanation: If the spread is out of control, the Xbar limits are not reliable.

5.2.4-1.stem: A u chart has ū = 0.40 defects per unit and an average subgroup size of 25. What are the limits (rounded to two decimals)?

5.2.4-2.stem: A c chart tracks defects on identical panels, with an average of 16 defects per panel. What are the control limits?

5.2.5-1.stem: A p chart has p̄ = 0.04 and an average subgroup size of 300. What are the limits?

5.2.6-1.stem: Samples of n = 100 are inspected, and the long-run defective rate is p̄ = 0.05. What are the np chart limits?
5.2.6-1.explanation: np̄ = 5. √(100 × 0.05 × 0.95) = 2.18. Three times that is 6.54. UCL = 11.54. The computed LCL is negative, so it is set to 0.

5.2.7-1.stem: Subgroups of n = 10 give X̿ = 50 and S̄ = 2. What are the Xbar chart limits and the S chart UCL?

5.2.8-1.stem: A team wants to detect a small, persistent drift in the mean that a regular Shewhart chart is likely to miss. Which charts are appropriate?
5.2.8-1.explanation: CuSum and EWMA accumulate small shifts and detect them faster than Shewhart charts.

5.2.8-2.stem: Using the Reference Document's standardized CuSum, Sₙ = (1 ÷ σ) × Σ(xᵢ − T), a process has target T = 50 and σ = 2. The readings are 52, 51, and 53. What is S₃?

5.2.9-1.stem: An EWMA chart uses λ = 0.3 with a starting value of 100. The first two readings are 110 and 106. What is EWMA₂?

5.2.10-1.stem: A control chart shows nine consecutive points above the center line, all inside the control limits. What is the correct reading?

options.html: The process is in control, because no point is outside the limits
A likely shift in the process mean; investigate for a special cause
A false alarm that should be ignored

5.2.10-1.explanation: Nine in a row on one side is a Nelson signal for a shift, even without any point beyond the limits.

5.2.10-2.stem: Two of three consecutive points fall beyond 2σ on the same side of the center line. Which rule is this?

options.html: Two of three beyond 2σ (a Western Electric and Nelson signal)
Eight in a row on one side

5.2.10-2.explanation: This is the "two of three beyond 2σ, same side" rule.

5.2.10-3.stem: If all points on a control chart are inside the control limits, the process is proven to be in control.
5.2.10-3.explanation: A pattern inside the limits can still violate a run or trend rule.

5.2.10-4.stem: A point falls beyond the upper limit. The technician finds a known tool breakage and wants to delete the point and recalculate the limits right away. What is the best response?

options.html: Delete it immediately to make the chart look in control
Investigate and correct the cause, then recompute limits only after a verified process change and a stable baseline

5.2.10-4.explanation: Do not recompute limits just because a point is out of control. Investigate the assignable cause first.

5.2.10-5.stem: On a control chart, Zone B lies between which distances from the center line?
5.2.10-5.explanation: Zone C is center to 1σ, Zone B is 1σ to 2σ, and Zone A is 2σ to 3σ.

5.2.10-6.stem: Control limits are the same thing as specification limits.
5.2.10-6.explanation: Control limits come from the process. Specification limits come from the customer.

options.html: Western Electric uses 8 points in a row on one side of the center line
Nelson (Minitab) uses 9 points in a row on one side of the center line
Both use 5 points in a row
Both use 15 points in a row

5.2.10-7.explanation: They are different rule systems, not contradictions. Use one set per question.
